PUBLIC SAFETY OFFICERS PROCEDURAL BILL OF RIGHTS ACT (POBR) — TERMINATION AND ADMINISTRATIVE APPEAL INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · City of Example Police Department

INFORMATION AND BACKGROUND — PUBLIC SAFETY OFFICERS PROCEDURAL BILL OF RIGHTS ACT AT TERMINATION
I, Jordan Lee, am completing this information sheet in connection with my employment as Police Officer II with City of Example Police Department. This information sheet describes the Public Safety Officers Procedural Bill of Rights Act (POBR), California Government Code sections 3300 through 3313 — a chapter of statutes that applies specifically to peace officers within the meaning of the Penal Code sections it cross-references, and that provides procedural rights connected to interrogation, punitive action (including dismissal), administrative appeal, personnel-file entries, and enforcement, separate from the wrongful-termination and general personnel-record doctrines this project addresses elsewhere. It is not an administrative appeal, a request for a Skelly-type hearing, a personnel-file correction request, or a superior court filing, and completing it does not initiate, extend, or preserve any deadline under Government Code section 3304, section 3306, section 3306.5, or any other statute or memorandum of understanding. Completing it does not establish that City of Example Police Department took, or failed to take, any specific action described in this sheet, or that any statement here is true.

WHO POBR COVERS: THE STATUTE'S OWN DEFINITION OF 'PUBLIC SAFETY OFFICER'
The Public Safety Officers Procedural Bill of Rights Act defines its own scope by cross-reference to the Penal Code's peace-officer classification statutes, rather than by reference to any generic notion of a 'public employee' or 'government worker.' For purposes of the chapter, the term 'public safety officer' means all peace officers specified in a listed set of Penal Code sections, with two of those cross-referenced sections carrying their own internal exceptions for a particular subdivision. The Legislature's own findings, stated in this same section, describe the chapter's rights as a matter of statewide concern grounded in the need for stable employer-employee relations in law enforcement, and direct that the chapter applies to every public safety officer as so defined wherever situated within California.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "the term public safety officer means all peace officers specified in Sections 830.1, 830.2, 830.3, 830.31, 830.32, 830.33, except subdivision (e), 830.34, 830.35, except subdivision (c), 830.36, 830.37, 830.38, 830.4, and 830.5 of the Penal Code."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 3301 (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, Public Safety Officers Procedural Bill of Rights Act, definition of public safety officer (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=3301.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only the cross-reference itself; it does not independently look up or restate what job classifications each cross-referenced Penal Code section (830.1, 830.2, 830.3, 830.31, 830.32, 830.33, 830.34, 830.35, 830.36, 830.37, 830.38, 830.4, and 830.5) actually covers, or resolve the two internal subdivision exceptions the statute itself carries (an exception within 830.33 and a different exception within 830.35). Whether a particular job title or appointment falls within one of those cross-referenced categories is a fact- and title-specific question this clause does not resolve. This chapter, and this document, do not extend to public employees generally — only to peace officers within this specific statutory definition; a different state civil-service employee, or a non-sworn public employee, is not necessarily covered by POBR even though both work for a government employer, and this clause does not determine that any specific job classification is or is not covered.

THE STATUTE'S OWN DEFINITION OF 'PUNITIVE ACTION'
POBR's protections connected to interrogation, administrative appeal, and the other rights this document describes are keyed to the statute's own defined term, 'punitive action.' The chapter states that, for its purposes, punitive action means any action that may lead to dismissal, demotion, suspension, reduction in salary, written reprimand, or transfer for purposes of punishment. Dismissal — the termination of a public safety officer's employment — is expressly listed as one form of punitive action within this definition, which is why POBR's administrative-appeal, investigation-deadline, and enforcement provisions reach a proposed or completed termination.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "For the purpose of this chapter, punitive action means any action that may lead to dismissal, demotion, suspension, reduction in salary, written reprimand, or transfer for purposes of punishment."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 3303 (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, Public Safety Officers Procedural Bill of Rights Act, definition of punitive action (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=3303.)
  Known gap: The definition covers a transfer only when it is 'for purposes of punishment'; it does not state how to distinguish a punitive transfer from an ordinary operational reassignment, and this clause does not resolve that line-drawing question for any specific transfer. The same is true of a 'reduction in salary' that results from a routine, non-disciplinary pay-scale change versus one imposed as discipline. This clause states the statute's own definitional text; it does not determine that any specific action taken against any particular public safety officer was, or was not, punitive action within this definition.

RIGHT TO REPRESENTATION DURING AN INTERROGATION THAT COULD LEAD TO PUNITIVE ACTION
When a formal written statement of charges has been filed, or when an interrogation focuses on matters likely to result in punitive action — which, as described above, includes dismissal — against a public safety officer, that officer has the right, on request, to be represented by a representative of their own choice, who may be present throughout the interrogation. The representative cannot be a person who is also subject to the same investigation, and cannot be required to disclose, or punished for refusing to disclose, information received from the officer in a noncriminal matter. The same statutory section states that this representation right, along with the rest of section 3303's interrogation conditions, does not apply to an officer's normal-course-of-duty supervisory contact, counseling, instruction, or informal verbal admonishment, and does not apply to an investigation concerned solely and directly with alleged criminal activity.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Upon the filing of a formal written statement of charges, or whenever an interrogation focuses on matters that are likely to result in punitive action against any public safety officer, that officer, at his or her request, shall have the right to be represented by a representative of his or her choice who may be present at all times during the interrogation."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 3303(i) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, right to a representative during an interrogation likely to result in punitive action (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=3303.)
  "This section shall not apply to any interrogation of a public safety officer in the normal course of duty, counseling, instruction, or informal verbal admonishment by, or other routine or unplanned contact with, a supervisor or any other public safety officer, nor shall this section apply to an investigation concerned solely and directly with alleged criminal activities."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 3303 (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, carve-out for routine supervisory contact and purely criminal investigations (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=3303.)
  Known gap: The statute conditions the representation right on the interrogation 'focus[ing] on matters that are likely to result in punitive action'; it does not itself define how imminent or certain that likelihood must be before the right attaches, and this clause does not resolve that question for any specific conversation. It also carves the right out entirely for an investigation 'concerned solely and directly with alleged criminal activities' without further defining that phrase, and does not address how a mixed administrative-and-criminal investigation is treated. CourtListener's daily search quota was exhausted when this document was researched (a 429 rate-limit response reporting 125 requests/day used), so no case law interpreting these phrases was independently verified for this document; only the statute's own text is relied on here.

PROHIBITION ON PUNITIVE ACTION FOR EXERCISING POBR OR GRIEVANCE RIGHTS
Separately from the administrative-appeal and investigation-deadline protections described elsewhere in this document, POBR itself prohibits subjecting a public safety officer to punitive action, denying the officer a promotion, or threatening either of those, because the officer lawfully exercised a right granted by this chapter or a right under an existing administrative grievance procedure. The same section clarifies that this protection does not stop an agency head from ordering an officer to cooperate with other agencies on criminal investigations, and that an officer who fails to comply with such an order may be officially charged with insubordination.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "No public safety officer shall be subjected to punitive action, or denied promotion, or be threatened with any such treatment, because of the lawful exercise of the rights granted under this chapter, or the exercise of any rights under any existing administrative grievance procedure."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 3304(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, prohibition on punitive action for exercising POBR or grievance rights (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=3304.)
  Known gap: The statute's text does not itself state the causation standard a public safety officer would need to show to establish that a punitive action was taken 'because of' the exercise of a chapter right or grievance right — for example, whether the protected exercise must be the sole cause, a substantial motivating factor, or merely a contributing factor. That causation-standard question is the kind of issue ordinarily resolved by case law, and CourtListener's daily search quota was exhausted when this document was researched, so no case law on this point was independently verified; only the statute's own text is relied on here.

RIGHT TO AN OPPORTUNITY FOR ADMINISTRATIVE APPEAL BEFORE PUNITIVE ACTION, INCLUDING DISMISSAL
POBR states directly that no punitive action — a category that, as described elsewhere in this document, includes dismissal — and no denial of promotion on grounds other than merit, may be undertaken by a public agency against a public safety officer who has successfully completed the applicable probationary period, without providing that officer an opportunity for administrative appeal. This is the statute's core procedural protection against termination without process: before a permanent (non-probationary) public safety officer's dismissal becomes final, the officer must be given an opportunity to appeal it administratively.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "No punitive action, nor denial of promotion on grounds other than merit, shall be undertaken by any public agency
 against any public safety officer who has successfully completed the probationary period that may be required by his or her employing agency without providing the public safety officer with an opportunity for administrative appeal."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 3304(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, right to an opportunity for administrative appeal before punitive action (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=3304.)
  Known gap: This right, by its own terms, applies only to a public safety officer who 'has successfully completed the probationary period that may be required by his or her employing agency' — the statute does not itself extend the same administrative-appeal guarantee to a probationary officer, and this clause does not determine whether a particular officer's probationary period, if any, had been completed at the relevant time. The statute also does not itself prescribe the procedure, format, or forum for the 'opportunity for administrative appeal' it requires; those details are typically set by the employing agency's own rules, a memorandum of understanding, or (for a chief of police specifically) the separate procedure in subdivision (c) of this same section, which this clause does not address.

ONE-YEAR DEADLINE TO COMPLETE AN INVESTIGATION AND NOTIFY THE OFFICER OF PROPOSED DISCIPLINE, AND ITS TOLLING EXCEPTIONS
Subject to specified exceptions, POBR bars a public agency from undertaking punitive action, or denying a promotion on grounds other than merit, for any act, omission, or other allegation of misconduct if the agency's investigation of that allegation is not completed within one year of the agency's discovery of the allegation by a person authorized to initiate an investigation. This one-year period applies only to misconduct occurring on or after January 1, 1998. Where the agency determines that discipline may be taken, the statute requires it to complete its investigation and notify the officer of the proposed discipline, by a Letter of Intent or Notice of Adverse Action, within that same year — but the statute does not require the agency to have actually imposed the discipline within the year, only to have completed the investigation and given that notice. The statute also lists specific circumstances that toll (pause) the one-year clock; among them, a pending criminal investigation or prosecution of the same act, omission, or allegation tolls the period for as long as that criminal matter is pending, and an officer may separately toll the period for a specified time by waiving it in writing.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "no punitive action, nor denial of promotion on grounds other than merit, shall be undertaken for any act, omission, or other allegation of misconduct if the investigation of the allegation is not completed within one year of the public agency’s discovery by a person authorized to initiate an investigation of the allegation of an act, omission, or other misconduct. This one-year limitation period shall apply only if the act, omission, or other misconduct occurred on or after January 1, 1998."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 3304(d)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, one-year deadline to complete investigation and notify officer of proposed discipline (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=3304.)
  "The public agency shall not be required to impose the discipline within that one-year period."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 3304(d)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, one-year deadline does not require discipline to be imposed within the year (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=3304.)
  "If the act, omission, or other allegation of misconduct is also the subject of a criminal investigation or criminal prosecution, the time during which the criminal investigation or criminal prosecution is pending shall toll the one-year time period."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 3304(d)(2)(A) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, tolling of the one-year deadline during a pending criminal investigation or prosecution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=3304.)
  "If the public safety officer waives the one-year time period in writing, the time period shall be tolled for the period of time specified in the written waiver."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 3304(d)(2)(B) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, tolling of the one-year deadline by the officer's written waiver (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=3304.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes and describes only two of the statute's listed tolling grounds — a pending criminal investigation/prosecution, and a written waiver by the officer. The same subdivision lists additional, separately enumerated tolling grounds this clause does not quote: a multijurisdictional investigation requiring a reasonable extension, an investigation involving more than one employee requiring a reasonable extension, an investigation involving an incapacitated or otherwise unavailable employee, an investigation involving a matter in civil litigation naming the officer as a party defendant, an investigation involving a matter in criminal litigation where the complainant is a criminal defendant, and an investigation involving an allegation of workers' compensation fraud by the officer. This clause also does not address the separate reopening-for-new-evidence exception found elsewhere in this same section, or the 30-day notice-of-decision requirement that applies once discipline is decided upon, both of which are outside this clause's scope.

RIGHT TO READ AND SIGN AN ADVERSE PERSONNEL COMMENT BEFORE ENTRY, AND TO FILE A 30-DAY WRITTEN RESPONSE
POBR restricts how an adverse personnel comment reaches a public safety officer's file. No comment adverse to a public safety officer's interest may be entered into that officer's personnel file, or any other file used for personnel purposes by the employer, unless the officer has first read and signed the instrument containing the comment, acknowledging awareness of it — except that the entry may still be made if the officer, after reading it, refuses to sign, in which case that refusal itself is noted on the document and signed or initialed by the officer. Separately, once an adverse comment is entered, the officer has 30 days within which to file a written response to it, and that written response must be attached to, and accompany, the adverse comment in the file going forward.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "No public safety officer shall have any comment adverse to his interest entered in his personnel file, or any other file used for any personnel purposes by his employer, without the public safety officer having first read and signed the instrument containing the adverse comment indicating he is aware of such comment, except that such entry may be made if after reading such instrument the public safety officer refuses to sign it."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 3305 (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, right to read and sign an adverse personnel comment before entry (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=3305.)
  "A public safety officer shall have 30 days within which to file a written response to any adverse comment entered in his personnel file. Such written response shall be attached to, and shall accompany, the adverse comment."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 3306 (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, 30-day right to file a written response to an adverse personnel comment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=3306.)
  Known gap: The statute does not itself define what makes a comment 'adverse' to an officer's interest, beyond the ordinary meaning of that phrase, and this clause does not resolve whether any specific comment about a particular officer would qualify. The right described here is a right to read, sign or note a refusal to sign, and to attach a written response — the statute's text quoted here does not itself state that filing a response causes the adverse comment to be removed, corrected, or given reduced weight; the personnel-file correction and inspection procedure in a separate section (addressed in a different clause of this document) is the mechanism this chapter provides for seeking correction or deletion of file material believed to be mistaken or unlawful.

RIGHT TO INSPECT THE PERSONNEL FILE USED TO DECIDE TERMINATION OR OTHER DISCIPLINE
POBR requires an employer, at reasonable times and reasonable intervals, on a public safety officer's request, during usual business hours, and with no loss of compensation to the officer, to permit that officer to inspect personnel files used or previously used to determine the officer's qualifications for employment, promotion, additional compensation, or termination or other disciplinary action. The statute also separately requires the employer to keep each officer's personnel file, or a true and correct copy of it, and to make the file or copy available within a reasonable period of time after the officer requests it. If, after examining the file, the officer believes a portion of it was mistakenly or unlawfully placed there, the officer may request in writing that it be corrected or deleted, describing the correction sought and the reasons for it; the employer then has 30 calendar days from that request to either grant it or state in writing its reasons for refusing, and either the officer's request or the employer's refusal becomes part of the personnel file.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Every employer shall, at reasonable times and at reasonable intervals, upon the request of a public safety officer, during usual business hours, with no loss of compensation to the officer, permit that officer to inspect personnel files that are used or have been used to determine that officer’s qualifications for employment, promotion, additional compensation, or termination or other disciplinary action."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 3306.5(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, right to inspect personnel files used to decide termination or discipline (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=3306.5.)
  "Each employer shall keep each public safety officer’s personnel file or a true and correct copy thereof , and shall make the file or copy thereof available within a reasonable period of time after a request therefor by the officer."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 3306.5(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, employer's duty to keep and make available the personnel file (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=3306.5.)
  Known gap: The statute requires inspection to occur 'at reasonable times and at reasonable intervals' and requires the file to be made available 'within a reasonable period of time' after a request — neither phrase is defined by a specific number of days in this section, unlike the 30-calendar-day deadline that applies once an officer has actually requested correction or deletion of file material. This clause does not resolve what interval or delay would, or would not, be 'reasonable' in any specific case, and does not address how this personnel-file inspection right interacts with the general (non-POBR) personnel-record inspection statute this corpus addresses in a separate Personnel and Payroll Record Retention Duration document and Employee's Request to Inspect Personnel and Payroll Records document, which apply more broadly to employees generally rather than specifically to public safety officers under this chapter.

ENFORCEMENT: SUPERIOR COURT JURISDICTION, INJUNCTIVE RELIEF, AND A CIVIL PENALTY FOR MALICIOUS VIOLATIONS
POBR gives the superior court initial jurisdiction over any proceeding a public safety officer brings against a public safety department for an alleged violation of the chapter. Where the court finds a violation, the statute directs it to render appropriate injunctive or other extraordinary relief to remedy the violation and prevent future violations of a like or similar nature, including a temporary restraining order, preliminary injunction, or permanent injunction prohibiting the department from taking punitive action against the officer. Beyond that injunctive relief, if the court finds that the department, or its employees, agents, or assigns acting within the scope of employment, maliciously violated a chapter provision with intent to injure the officer, the statute makes the department liable, for each violation, for a civil penalty of up to $25,000 awarded to the officer whose right was denied, plus reasonable attorney's fees as the court determines, and for actual damages where the evidence establishes them.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The superior court shall have initial jurisdiction over any proceeding brought by any public safety officer against any public safety department for alleged violations of this chapter."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 3309.5(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, superior court's initial jurisdiction over POBR violations (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=3309.5.)
  "the court shall render appropriate injunctive or other extraordinary relief to remedy the violation and to prevent future violations of a like or similar nature, including, but not limited to, the granting of a temporary restraining order, preliminary injunction, or permanent injunction prohibiting the public safety department from taking any punitive action against the public safety officer."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 3309.5(d)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, injunctive and extraordinary relief for a POBR violation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=3309.5.)
  "upon a finding by a superior court that a public safety department, its employees, agents, or assigns, with respect to acts taken within the scope of employment, maliciously violated any provision of this chapter with the intent to injure the public safety officer, the public safety department shall, for each and every violation, be liable for a civil penalty not to exceed twenty-five thousand dollars ($25,000) to be awarded to the public safety officer whose right or protection was denied and for reasonable attorney’s fees as may be determined by the court."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 3309.5(e) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code, civil penalty up to $25,000 for a malicious POBR violation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=3309.5.)
  Known gap: The $25,000-per-violation civil penalty and fee-shifting remedy require the heightened showing that the violation was done 'maliciously' and 'with the intent to injure the public safety officer' — the ordinary injunctive relief available under subdivision (d)(1) does not require that showing, and this clause does not resolve where the line falls between an ordinary (non-malicious) violation and a malicious one. CourtListener's daily search quota was exhausted when this document was researched, so no case law construing 'maliciously violated ... with the intent to injure' was independently verified for this document; only the statute's own text is relied on here. This clause also does not address the statute's separate sanctions provision for a bad-faith or frivolous filing under this chapter, or any residual statute of limitations that might apply to filing such a proceeding, which this section's text does not itself state.

CLOSING AND SIGNATURE BLOCK — POBR AT TERMINATION INFORMATION SHEET
I declare that the information above is true and correct to the best of my knowledge.

Executed on September 6, 2026 at Sacramento, California.

Signature of Jordan Lee: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet describes the Public Safety Officers Procedural Bill of Rights Act, California Government Code sections 3301, 3303, 3304, 3305, 3306, 3306.5, and 3309.5 — the statute's own definitions of "public safety officer" and "punitive action" (including dismissal), the interrogation-representation right, the prohibition on punitive action for exercising chapter or grievance rights, the right to an opportunity for administrative appeal before punitive action against a non-probationary officer, the one-year deadline (and certain tolling grounds) to complete an investigation and notify the officer of proposed discipline, the right to read, sign, and respond in writing to an adverse personnel comment, the right to inspect and obtain the personnel file used to decide termination or discipline, and the superior court enforcement mechanism including its civil penalty for a malicious violation. It does not itself determine that City of Example Police Department did, or did not, comply with any provision of this chapter with respect to Jordan Lee, is not an administrative appeal, grievance, personnel-file correction request, or court filing, is not filed with any agency or court by completing it, does not constitute legal advice, and is not a substitute for consulting the actual statute, the employing agency's own rules or applicable memorandum of understanding, or a licensed attorney.]

expectedJSON.body: Separately from the administrative-appeal and investigation-deadline protections described elsewhere in this document, POBR itself prohibits subjecting a public safety officer to punitive action, denying the officer a promotion, or threatening either of those, because the officer lawfully exercised a right granted by this chapter or a right under an existing administrative grievance procedure. The same section clarifies that this protection does not stop an agency head from ordering an officer to cooperate with other agencies on criminal investigations, and that an officer who fails to comply with such an order may be officially charged with insubordination.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 3304(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, prohibition on punitive action for exercising POBR or grievance rights
citations.quote: No public safety officer shall be subjected to punitive action, or denied promotion, or be threatened with any such treatment, because of the lawful exercise of the rights granted under this chapter, or the exercise of any rights under any existing administrative grievance procedure.

expectedJSON.gap: The statute's text does not itself state the causation standard a public safety officer would need to show to establish that a punitive action was taken 'because of' the exercise of a chapter right or grievance right — for example, whether the protected exercise must be the sole cause, a substantial motivating factor, or merely a contributing factor. That causation-standard question is the kind of issue ordinarily resolved by case law, and CourtListener's daily search quota was exhausted when this document was researched, so no case law on this point was independently verified; only the statute's own text is relied on here.

expectedJSON.body: POBR states directly that no punitive action — a category that, as described elsewhere in this document, includes dismissal — and no denial of promotion on grounds other than merit, may be undertaken by a public agency against a public safety officer who has successfully completed the applicable probationary period, without providing that officer an opportunity for administrative appeal. This is the statute's core procedural protection against termination without process: before a permanent (non-probationary) public safety officer's dismissal becomes final, the officer must be given an opportunity to appeal it administratively.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 3304(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, right to an opportunity for administrative appeal before punitive action
citations.quote:
No punitive action, nor denial of promotion on grounds other than merit, shall be undertaken by any public agency
 against any public safety officer who has successfully completed the probationary period that may be required by his or her employing agency without providing the public safety officer with an opportunity for administrative appeal.

expectedJSON.gap: This right, by its own terms, applies only to a public safety officer who 'has successfully completed the probationary period that may be required by his or her employing agency' — the statute does not itself extend the same administrative-appeal guarantee to a probationary officer, and this clause does not determine whether a particular officer's probationary period, if any, had been completed at the relevant time. The statute also does not itself prescribe the procedure, format, or forum for the 'opportunity for administrative appeal' it requires; those details are typically set by the employing agency's own rules, a memorandum of understanding, or (for a chief of police specifically) the separate procedure in subdivision (c) of this same section, which this clause does not address.

expectedJSON.body: Subject to specified exceptions, POBR bars a public agency from undertaking punitive action, or denying a promotion on grounds other than merit, for any act, omission, or other allegation of misconduct if the agency's investigation of that allegation is not completed within one year of the agency's discovery of the allegation by a person authorized to initiate an investigation. This one-year period applies only to misconduct occurring on or after January 1, 1998. Where the agency determines that discipline may be taken, the statute requires it to complete its investigation and notify the officer of the proposed discipline, by a Letter of Intent or Notice of Adverse Action, within that same year — but the statute does not require the agency to have actually imposed the discipline within the year, only to have completed the investigation and given that notice. The statute also lists specific circumstances that toll (pause) the one-year clock; among them, a pending criminal investigation or prosecution of the same act, omission, or allegation tolls the period for as long as that criminal matter is pending, and an officer may separately toll the period for a specified time by waiving it in writing.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 3304(d)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, one-year deadline to complete investigation and notify officer of proposed discipline
citations.quote: no punitive action, nor denial of promotion on grounds other than merit, shall be undertaken for any act, omission, or other allegation of misconduct if the investigation of the allegation is not completed within one year of the public agency’s discovery by a person authorized to initiate an investigation of the allegation of an act, omission, or other misconduct. This one-year limitation period shall apply only if the act, omission, or other misconduct occurred on or after January 1, 1998.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 3304(d)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, one-year deadline does not require discipline to be imposed within the year
citations.quote: The public agency shall not be required to impose the discipline within that one-year period.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 3304(d)(2)(A) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, tolling of the one-year deadline during a pending criminal investigation or prosecution
citations.quote: If the act, omission, or other allegation of misconduct is also the subject of a criminal investigation or criminal prosecution, the time during which the criminal investigation or criminal prosecution is pending shall toll the one-year time period.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 3304(d)(2)(B) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, tolling of the one-year deadline by the officer's written waiver
citations.quote: If the public safety officer waives the one-year time period in writing, the time period shall be tolled for the period of time specified in the written waiver.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause quotes and describes only two of the statute's listed tolling grounds — a pending criminal investigation/prosecution, and a written waiver by the officer. The same subdivision lists additional, separately enumerated tolling grounds this clause does not quote: a multijurisdictional investigation requiring a reasonable extension, an investigation involving more than one employee requiring a reasonable extension, an investigation involving an incapacitated or otherwise unavailable employee, an investigation involving a matter in civil litigation naming the officer as a party defendant, an investigation involving a matter in criminal litigation where the complainant is a criminal defendant, and an investigation involving an allegation of workers' compensation fraud by the officer. This clause also does not address the separate reopening-for-new-evidence exception found elsewhere in this same section, or the 30-day notice-of-decision requirement that applies once discipline is decided upon, both of which are outside this clause's scope.

expectedJSON.body: POBR restricts how an adverse personnel comment reaches a public safety officer's file. No comment adverse to a public safety officer's interest may be entered into that officer's personnel file, or any other file used for personnel purposes by the employer, unless the officer has first read and signed the instrument containing the comment, acknowledging awareness of it — except that the entry may still be made if the officer, after reading it, refuses to sign, in which case that refusal itself is noted on the document and signed or initialed by the officer. Separately, once an adverse comment is entered, the officer has 30 days within which to file a written response to it, and that written response must be attached to, and accompany, the adverse comment in the file going forward.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 3305 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, right to read and sign an adverse personnel comment before entry
citations.quote: No public safety officer shall have any comment adverse to his interest entered in his personnel file, or any other file used for any personnel purposes by his employer, without the public safety officer having first read and signed the instrument containing the adverse comment indicating he is aware of such comment, except that such entry may be made if after reading such instrument the public safety officer refuses to sign it.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 3306 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, 30-day right to file a written response to an adverse personnel comment
citations.quote: A public safety officer shall have 30 days within which to file a written response to any adverse comment entered in his personnel file. Such written response shall be attached to, and shall accompany, the adverse comment.

expectedJSON.gap: The statute does not itself define what makes a comment 'adverse' to an officer's interest, beyond the ordinary meaning of that phrase, and this clause does not resolve whether any specific comment about a particular officer would qualify. The right described here is a right to read, sign or note a refusal to sign, and to attach a written response — the statute's text quoted here does not itself state that filing a response causes the adverse comment to be removed, corrected, or given reduced weight; the personnel-file correction and inspection procedure in a separate section (addressed in a different clause of this document) is the mechanism this chapter provides for seeking correction or deletion of file material believed to be mistaken or unlawful.

expectedJSON.body: POBR requires an employer, at reasonable times and reasonable intervals, on a public safety officer's request, during usual business hours, and with no loss of compensation to the officer, to permit that officer to inspect personnel files used or previously used to determine the officer's qualifications for employment, promotion, additional compensation, or termination or other disciplinary action. The statute also separately requires the employer to keep each officer's personnel file, or a true and correct copy of it, and to make the file or copy available within a reasonable period of time after the officer requests it. If, after examining the file, the officer believes a portion of it was mistakenly or unlawfully placed there, the officer may request in writing that it be corrected or deleted, describing the correction sought and the reasons for it; the employer then has 30 calendar days from that request to either grant it or state in writing its reasons for refusing, and either the officer's request or the employer's refusal becomes part of the personnel file.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 3306.5(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, right to inspect personnel files used to decide termination or discipline
citations.quote: Every employer shall, at reasonable times and at reasonable intervals, upon the request of a public safety officer, during usual business hours, with no loss of compensation to the officer, permit that officer to inspect personnel files that are used or have been used to determine that officer’s qualifications for employment, promotion, additional compensation, or termination or other disciplinary action.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 3306.5(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, employer's duty to keep and make available the personnel file
citations.quote: Each employer shall keep each public safety officer’s personnel file or a true and correct copy thereof , and shall make the file or copy thereof available within a reasonable period of time after a request therefor by the officer.

expectedJSON.gap: The statute requires inspection to occur 'at reasonable times and at reasonable intervals' and requires the file to be made available 'within a reasonable period of time' after a request — neither phrase is defined by a specific number of days in this section, unlike the 30-calendar-day deadline that applies once an officer has actually requested correction or deletion of file material. This clause does not resolve what interval or delay would, or would not, be 'reasonable' in any specific case, and does not address how this personnel-file inspection right interacts with the general (non-POBR) personnel-record inspection statute this corpus addresses in a separate Personnel and Payroll Record Retention Duration document and Employee's Request to Inspect Personnel and Payroll Records document, which apply more broadly to employees generally rather than specifically to public safety officers under this chapter.

expectedJSON.body: POBR gives the superior court initial jurisdiction over any proceeding a public safety officer brings against a public safety department for an alleged violation of the chapter. Where the court finds a violation, the statute directs it to render appropriate injunctive or other extraordinary relief to remedy the violation and prevent future violations of a like or similar nature, including a temporary restraining order, preliminary injunction, or permanent injunction prohibiting the department from taking punitive action against the officer. Beyond that injunctive relief, if the court finds that the department, or its employees, agents, or assigns acting within the scope of employment, maliciously violated a chapter provision with intent to injure the officer, the statute makes the department liable, for each violation, for a civil penalty of up to $25,000 awarded to the officer whose right was denied, plus reasonable attorney's fees as the court determines, and for actual damages where the evidence establishes them.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 3309.5(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, superior court's initial jurisdiction over POBR violations
citations.quote: The superior court shall have initial jurisdiction over any proceeding brought by any public safety officer against any public safety department for alleged violations of this chapter.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 3309.5(d)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, injunctive and extraordinary relief for a POBR violation
citations.quote: the court shall render appropriate injunctive or other extraordinary relief to remedy the violation and to prevent future violations of a like or similar nature, including, but not limited to, the granting of a temporary restraining order, preliminary injunction, or permanent injunction prohibiting the public safety department from taking any punitive action against the public safety officer.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 3309.5(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, civil penalty up to $25,000 for a malicious POBR violation
citations.quote: upon a finding by a superior court that a public safety department, its employees, agents, or assigns, with respect to acts taken within the scope of employment, maliciously violated any provision of this chapter with the intent to injure the public safety officer, the public safety department shall, for each and every violation, be liable for a civil penalty not to exceed twenty-five thousand dollars ($25,000) to be awarded to the public safety officer whose right or protection was denied and for reasonable attorney’s fees as may be determined by the court.

expectedJSON.gap: The $25,000-per-violation civil penalty and fee-shifting remedy require the heightened showing that the violation was done 'maliciously' and 'with the intent to injure the public safety officer' — the ordinary injunctive relief available under subdivision (d)(1) does not require that showing, and this clause does not resolve where the line falls between an ordinary (non-malicious) violation and a malicious one. CourtListener's daily search quota was exhausted when this document was researched, so no case law construing 'maliciously violated ... with the intent to injure' was independently verified for this document; only the statute's own text is relied on here. This clause also does not address the statute's separate sanctions provision for a bad-faith or frivolous filing under this chapter, or any residual statute of limitations that might apply to filing such a proceeding, which this section's text does not itself state.
